Volume 08 · Chapter 03

Valuation models and terminal assumptions

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v08-c02

By the endValue an operating business using explicit growth and reinvestment economics.

Capability and prerequisites

After this chapter, you can value an operating business from an explicit capital and earnings path, explain what a continuation value assumes, and distinguish growth that creates value from growth that consumes it. Read free cash flow and discounting, including the operating-value/equity bridge and nominal, currency and timing conventions. Keep the incremental NPV reasoning of capital budgeting and the stock-flow discipline of three-statement forecasting. Discount rates here are supplied appropriate rates for the stipulated cash claims; the next chapter develops their estimation and limitations.

A forecast can contain elaborate annual detail and still depend on one unsupported final cell. The remedy is to connect that cell to the business: what productive resources survive, what cash must be reinvested, what return new investment earns, and why margins or competitive advantages persist. More forecast columns do not establish those facts. A terminal assumption describes the business after the spreadsheet stops showing individual years.

1. A continuation value has a date and a cash-flow boundary

Let Ft be free cash flow to the firm, FCFF, paid at the end of year t. It is after operating tax and required operating reinvestment but before payments to financing claimants. V0 is operating value just after any date-0 distributions. With a constant appropriate annual rate r and an explicit horizon H,

V0 = Σt=1…H Ft/(1+r)t + TVH/(1+r)H.
TVH = value at date H of cash flows beginning at date H+1.

Thus FH and TVH occur at the same valuation date but cover different cash. TVH excludes the distribution FH that the explicit sum already includes. It is not automatically proceeds from a sale, liquidation or an additional asset. If a buyer acquires exactly the remaining operating claim at H, its modeled price could equal TVH; adding both would count the same claim twice. With varying appropriate rates, discount through the product of the relevant annual gross factors; a single constant r is an assumption, not an accounting identity.

Suppose the first continuation cash is FH+1 and later cash grows at g. For r > −1 and g > −1, the discounted series is geometric, with ratio q = (1+g)/(1+r). When g < r,

TVH = [FH+1/(1+r)] Σj=0…∞ qj = FH+1/(r−g).

For positive continuing cash, g ≥ r makes this series fail to converge; a negative denominator is not a defensible negative valuation from the same cash stream. A finite-life operation instead needs its remaining finite cash and an explicit net closure or disposal amount. Damodaran's terminal-value chapter distinguishes a going-concern continuation from liquidation and a market-based exit multiple. A multiple estimated from other companies is additional market evidence with its own comparability assumptions, developed later in this volume.

Worked example 1 — Which cash belongs in the numerator?

A separate fictional operating forecast supplies FCFF of 24 kCU in year 1 and 32 kCU in year 2. A separately supported continuation plan, already after its reinvestment, supplies 33.28 kCU in year 3 and 4% growth thereafter. The compatible nominal CU discount rate is 12%. These are hypothetical assumptions, not current market estimates.

At date 2, TV2 = 33.28/(0.12 − 0.04) = 416. Therefore V0 = 24/1.12 + (32 + 416)/1.12² = 2650/7 ≈ 378.571 kCU. The terminal component's present value is 16250/49 ≈ 331.633; its share of operating value is 325/371 ≈ 87.60%. Using 32 instead of the already supplied next-year cash shifts the boundary backward. Discounting TV2 for three years shifts its valuation date forward. Adding a separate sale of 416 at date 2 would duplicate the continuation.

The arithmetic checks the dates. It does not show that 33.28 can be sustained after capital spending, that 4% can persist indefinitely, or that 12% properly prices the risk. We next expose those operating assumptions.

2. Growth must have an earnings and capital mechanism

Write Nt for NOPAT, net operating profit after tax, before financing interest. Let Kt−1 be operating invested capital at the beginning of year t. It comprises net operating long-lived assets plus operating working capital, excluding excess cash and financing debt. In our clean capital model, there are no acquisition, currency, impairment, revaluation or other noncash capital changes. End-year net reinvestment It is

It = Capext − D&At + ΔOperating NWCt;
Kt = Kt−1 + It;   Ft = Nt − It.

Those equations require the same perimeter and accounting treatment throughout. An acquisition's added capital cannot be inserted while its purchase payment or earnings are omitted. Likewise, a write-down can reduce measured capital without releasing cash. An intangible-intensive business may need consistent treatment of investment that its accounting statements expense. Capital measurement and the supporting earnings must be adjusted together.

For Nt > 0, define bt = It/Nt, the net reinvestment rate. It is not simply capex divided by profit: depreciation and working capital matter. Define ρnew,t+1 as the next year's incremental after-tax operating earnings per unit invested at date t. Let ΔNold,t+1 capture the change in next-year earnings from the capital already supporting Nt. Then, under this one-year implementation timing,

Nt+1 = Nt + ΔNold,t+1 + ρnew,t+1It;
gt+1 = ΔNold,t+1/Nt + ρnew,t+1bt.

The familiar g = ROIC × reinvestment rate follows only when the old capital's earnings are maintained and the specified return is the relevant return on new investment, with no omitted implementation lag. Replacement and maintenance spending must already be allowed for. Price increases, a turnaround, capacity utilization or competitive erosion can change earnings on old assets without being the return on this year's new investment. Those improvements may themselves require spending; the label “efficiency” does not make them free.

An average accounting return Nt/Kt−1 can reflect valuable old projects while new opportunities have poor returns. Conversely, temporarily depressed old assets can conceal a promising new project. Damodaran's discussion of fundamental growth separates average and marginal returns and the contribution of changing returns on existing capital. Our timing equations make that distinction explicit. Neither a favorable historical average nor a fitted growth rate replaces an incremental project forecast.

As a small illustration, N = 60 and net reinvestment 30 give b = 50%. If the new capital earns 8% and old earnings stay at 60, next N is 62.4 and growth is 4%, even if the historical average return was 20%. If old earnings instead fall by 6, next N is 56.4 and growth is −6%. Applying 20%×50% would have forecast 10% growth in both cases, missing both the marginal return and the deterioration.

3. Stable growth links the numerator and denominator

For a stable positive-NOPAT model, suppose operating returns on new investment are R > 0, old earnings are maintained, growth g is supported by b = g/R, and the operating rate r is appropriate for that continuing business. Then F = N(1−g/R). Holding the first continuing NOPAT N1 fixed, the value at the preceding date is

V(R,g,r;N1) = N1(1−g/R)/(r−g).

Here investment at the end of year 1 funds the increase from N1 to N2. A sensitivity exercise that fixes N1 must not silently change productive capacity before year 1. If the constant R applies to all opening capital, K0 = N1/R and K grows coherently with earnings. If only incremental returns are constant, legacy capital can have a different average return; that requires a separately described legacy earnings path.

For 0 ≤ g < r and 0 ≤ g ≤ R, this bounded version has 0 ≤ b ≤ 1 and nonnegative FCFF. Those inequalities express this model's internally financed reinvestment policy. Actual firms may invest more than NOPAT, shrink their assets, or have negative NOPAT, but then their funding, asset-release and earnings paths need explicit modeling. A ratio with zero or negative earnings does not supply the missing model.

Holding N1, R and r fixed:
∂V/∂g = N1(1−r/R)/(r−g)².

Thus more supported growth raises value if R > r, leaves it unchanged if R = r, and lowers it if R < r. Growth consumes current distributable cash; the later benefit must compensate for that investment. Damodaran's excess-return explanation makes the same reinvestment tradeoff. The conclusion depends on complete incremental cash economics, not on treating an unadjusted accounting ratio as a project's economic yield.

Worked example 2 — A larger business can have a smaller value

Three separate hypothetical businesses each have next-year NOPAT 96 kCU and r = 8%. Compare zero growth with 2% growth from year 1 onward, maintaining the first year's earnings within each comparison. Returns are maintained at the indicated R on all productive capital.

Original steady-state comparisons, kCU unless a percentage
ROpening K = 96/Rb at g = 2%First FCFFValue with g = 2%Value with g = 0
4%240050%488001200
8%120025%7212001200
16%60012.5%8414001200

For R = 4%, investing 48 out of NOPAT 96 generates next-year additional earnings of 1.92, so NOPAT grows 2%; the investment nevertheless earns less than the required 8%. Value falls by 400 relative to the no-growth alternative. At R = 8%, value is 96/0.08 = 1200 regardless of the admissible growth choice. At R = 16%, supported growth adds 200. Across rows, opening capital differs; these are not three estimates for an unchanged physical asset base. Within each row, the growth comparison holds that base and first-year NOPAT fixed.

One can increase a spreadsheet valuation by raising g while freezing FCFF. That changes the modeled reinvestment economics. It is not the comparison in this table.

4. Let competitive returns fade through a closed capital path

A fade is a specified transition in returns, margins, growth or other drivers toward a continuing regime. Its duration and shape need evidence about entry, contracts, product substitution, technology, customer switching and reinvestment opportunities. They are not supplied by choosing a standard spreadsheet horizon. Some advantages persist; assuming that they do so forever is a stronger claim than expecting another good year. The discussion of competitive-advantage periods in the terminal-value source motivates this question, without establishing the return path of our fictional firm.

For the following case, ρt applies to all capital productive in year t, including prior investments: Nt = ρtKt−1. Because investment happens at year-end,

Nt+1/Nt = (ρt+1/ρt)(1+btρt);
gt+1 = (ρt+1/ρt−1) + ρt+1bt.

The first term changes earnings on old capital; the second is the contribution of new investment. This is one explicit fade mechanism. A model in which old project returns are protected and only new-project returns fade would have a different capital-vintage earnings path and potentially a different value.

Worked example 3 — Mariner Calibration Services

Contract and units. Mariner Calibration Services is an original fictional business, separate from the Chapter 1 and Chapter 2 cases, with amounts in nominal kCU and annual end-date cash flows. Opening operating capital is 500, split into net PPE 400 and operating NWC 100. Excess cash is excluded. Sales in each year equal opening operating capital: sales/capital is one. NOPAT is the supplied return times opening capital; a fictional 25% operating tax rate is fully usable and paid in cash, so EBIT = NOPAT/0.75. Tax deductions match book depreciation. The supplied appropriate operating discount rate is 10%; no separate interest or tax-shield cash is added to this FCFF valuation.

Each year, depreciation is 5% of opening net PPE. The case policy replaces that book consumption through capex and directs 80% of additional net reinvestment to net PPE and 20% to operating NWC. Thus capex = depreciation + 0.8I and ΔNWC = 0.2I. This replacement equality is a maintained business assumption, not evidence that book depreciation always equals economic maintenance spending. No acquisitions, write-downs, currency changes or other capital movements occur. The model field called cash operating cost is sales minus EBIT minus depreciation; it means operating expense excluding D&A before working-capital settlement adjustments, not an independently observed supplier payment. The NWC bridge supplies those timing adjustments. This cost is nonnegative throughout the supplied path.

Revenue 572 less cash operating cost 457.6 and operating tax 22.88 leaves operating cash before working-capital timing and capex of 91.52; subtract capex and NWC absorption to obtain the same FCFF. Book expense, replacement cash and added capacity each enter once.

The boundary matters. Returns have reached the continuing 10% in year 4. Stable growth from year 4 to year 5 is 3%, so year 4 reinvestment already switches to b = 3%/10% = 30%. At date 4 this creates K4 = 606.8348. Therefore N5 = 10%×606.8348 = 60.68348 = 58.916×1.03. Year 5 reinvestment is 18.205044, leaving F5 = 42.478436. TV4 = 42.478436/(0.10−0.03) = 606.8348;

= 70340/121 ≈ 581.322314 kCU.

When continuing R = r, TV4 = N5/r = K4. Future reinvestment earns exactly the required return under the case model. Separately supplied date-0 excess-cash value is 30, nonoperating asset value 15 and the market value of the debt claim 200, with no other claims. Common equity value is 581.322314 + 30 + 15 − 200 = 51585/121 ≈ 426.322314 kCU. For 20 thousand ordinary shares, value is 10317/484 ≈ CU 21.316116 per share. Cash already needed within operating NWC is not added again; interest is not deducted again from FCFF. These supplied claim values and the rate convention describe a non-distress bridge, not a debt repayment model.

An independent value identity

Define economic profit EPt = Nt − rKt−1. Since Ft = Nt − (Kt − Kt−1), substitution gives Ft = EPt + (1+r)Kt−1 − Kt. Discounting and summing makes the adjacent capital terms cancel:

V0 = K0 + Σt=1…H EPt/(1+r)t + (TVH−KH)/(1+r)H.

Mariner Calibration Services's explicit economic profits are 50, 33, 11.44 and 0. Its terminal difference is zero. Hence V0 = 500 + 50/1.1 + 33/1.1² + 11.44/1.1³ = 581.322314, independently matching the cash valuation. This finite identity relies on the specified capital rollforward; it is not a claim that arbitrary accounting book values equal market value. Persistent book measurement errors change the apparent capital and economic-profit components even when a correctly reconstructed cash valuation is unchanged.

5. A valid denominator is only the first terminal constraint

A positive r−g proves convergence for the stated geometric cash stream. It does not establish that the stream can occur. Check the productive capital supporting next-year earnings, reinvestment sufficient for growth, achievable operating margins and turnover, maintenance needs, working-capital terms, usable taxes, the relevant market's capacity, and a financing/risk policy compatible with the chosen rate. Losses, a heavy refinancing requirement or changing leverage may require a longer explicit forecast and a different financing treatment.

A firm with a positive share of an addressable market cannot keep growing faster than that market forever at fixed comparable price and perimeter definitions: its modeled share would eventually exceed one. This is an asymptotic consistency check, not a forecast that every mature firm grows at GDP. The stable-growth discussion emphasizes the relevant economy and nominal/real and currency distinctions. We do not adopt its historical numerical examples or treat a growth-versus-risk-free-rate heuristic as a mathematical theorem. The cash-series convergence condition must be checked separately.

Negative long-run growth can describe gradual run-off if asset releases, maintenance, customer obligations and eventual closure are coherent; the general geometric formula permits −1 < g < r. A finite mine, expiring concession or product withdrawal may be better represented by explicit finite cash and net liquidation. Include disposal taxes, cleanup or severance, recoverable operating working capital and required settlement costs exactly once. Do not add liquidation of the same productive assets to a going-concern value that already relies on them.

Raising terminal ROIC requires a reason that incremental investment remains productive after competition, not merely a high historical average. Treat persistent excess returns as a separate scenario if the evidence is uncertain. Equally, a permanent low-return reinvestment policy may be economically poor without being arithmetically inconsistent; compare a credible reduction, sale or redeployment of that investment rather than assuming managers must pursue growth.

6. Sensitivity must rebuild the business it changes

The supplied lab varies r and g while maintaining Mariner Calibration Services's other stated operating assumptions. Changing g regenerates year 4 reinvestment, F4, K4, N5 and continuing FCFF. It does not freeze the old cash path and change only a denominator. Changing r changes both discounting and the interpretation of the continuing return spread. These are conditional scenarios, not estimated probabilities or confidence intervals.

Mariner Calibration Services operating value, kCU; terminal ROIC stays 10%
Supplied rg = 0%g = 3%g = 6%
8%728.365798.5191079.136
10%581.322581.322581.322
12%483.360460.063413.468

In the middle row, R = r: changing supported growth has no effect on value. In the first row, incremental return exceeds the assumed required rate and growth helps. In the last, the same 10% return is below a 12% requirement and growth hurts. At an already stable final explicit year, FH + TVH = NH(1+r)(1−g/R)/(r−g); the reinvestment at the boundary is essential to this comparison.

At the base case, the present value of TV4 is about 414.476334, or 71.298886% of operating value. That large share does not mean that most value comes from a perpetual competitive advantage: Mariner Calibration Services has no continuing excess return. It mainly reflects a capital base and normal-return cash that continue beyond the short explicit window. Moving two unchanged stable years into the explicit forecast lowers the terminal share without changing total value. Conversely, a low terminal share does not validate the explicit forecasts.

With a fixed positive numerator, approaching r = g magnifies the effect of small input changes. When reinvestment also changes, inspect the entire numerator and capital path. Report a defensible set of scenarios and which facts would distinguish them; a finely rounded single price should not conceal uncertain margins, capital needs or discount rates.

Reproduce and challenge the forecast

Download the original assumptions, standard-library benchmark, preserved exact output and experiment guide. Keep them together and run python3 v08-c03-analysis.py. Exact rational strings preserve the calculations; no installation, service or network is needed. The output includes operating statements, PPE/NWC paths, old/new earnings contributions, both value identities and the coherent sensitivity grid.

The lab deliberately requires positive NOPAT/ROIC, nonnegative reinvestment no larger than NOPAT, a final explicit ROIC matching the stable return, g < r and a nonnegative residual equity bridge. It rejects unsupported terminal jumps, negative implied cash operating costs and incompatible numeric inputs instead of silently clipping them. Those restrictions identify its teaching scope. They do not declare that every business outside the scope lacks value.

Exercises

All monetary amounts are kCU unless stated otherwise. Use annual end-date cash, exact intermediate values and the explicitly supplied rates. No current market observation is implied. Explain the operating or timing condition behind each formula.

  1. FCFF is 30 in year 1 and 40 in year 2. A separately supported reinvestment plan supplies FCFF 42 in year 3, then 2% growth thereafter; r = 8%. Find TV2 and V0. Quantify the present-value understatement from using 40 instead of 42 in the continuation numerator. Does this supplied first continuation year require 42/40−1 to equal the later 2% rate?
  2. A business has NOPAT 80 on opening capital 400 and reinvests 32 at year-end. The new capital earns 12.5% next year, while earnings from old capital decline by 6.4. Compute historical average ROIC, b, new-investment earnings, next NOPAT and total growth. Explain why neither average ROIC×b nor marginal ROIC×b alone gives total growth.
  3. A stable business has first-year NOPAT 72, return R = 18% on all capital and r = 12%. Compare g = 0%, 3% and 6%, holding first-year earnings and opening capital fixed. Calculate reinvestment, first FCFF and value. Verify the direction with the derivative and explain why the higher-growth case has lower current FCFF.
  4. A smaller version of the capital model opens with net PPE 240 and operating NWC 60. Year-1 ROIC is 15%, b is 40%, depreciation is 5% of opening PPE, and 80% of net investment goes to PPE. Find NOPAT, I, capex, ΔNWC, closing PPE/NWC/K and FCFF. Next-year return on all capital falls to 12%. Find next NOPAT and its growth, decomposed between old and new capital.
  5. Keep Mariner Calibration Services's entire base economics unchanged, but extend the explicit horizon from four to six years by writing out two years of its stable 10% return, 3% growth and 30% reinvestment. Compute FCFF in years 5–6, K6 and TV6. Verify at date 4 that the two explicit cash flows plus the new continuation equal the old TV4. What happens to today's operating value and terminal share?
  6. Keep Mariner Calibration Services's r = R = 10%, years 1–3 and NOPAT4 fixed. For g = 0%, 3% and 6%, compute year-4 I, FCFF, K4 and TV4. Prove that F4 + TV4 is unchanged. Explain the error in freezing year-4 reinvestment while claiming the new growth begins from year 4 to year 5.
  7. An analyst inserts positive first continuation cash 10, r = 7% and g = 8%, obtaining −1000 from the algebraic fraction. Is that a valid value of the stated perpetuity? Separately, a proposed internally financed stable case uses g = 3% and R = 2%. Find its implied b and explain what assumptions must change before it fits a defensible model. Give an appropriate alternative to a going-concern perpetuity for an operation whose contract ends in three years.
  8. A management packet forecasts first continuing NOPAT 50, R = 20%, g = 4% and r = 8%, but sets FCFF equal to NOPAT because “growth pays for itself.” Excess cash is 12, a separately valued nonoperating asset is 3, debt market value is 100 and shares are 10 thousand. Correct the cash/value/equity/per-share calculation and compare it with management's arithmetic. Identify four distinct evidence areas required before treating the corrected number as a defensible valuation, including at least one terminal-economics issue and one measurement/timing issue.
Complete exercise solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. TV2 = 42/(0.08−0.02) = 700. V0 = 30/1.08 + (40+700)/1.08² = 482750/729 ≈ 662.208505. The wrong numerator reduces date-2 continuation by 2/0.06 = 100/3 and present value by 62500/2187 ≈ 28.578. The 5% jump from 40 to 42 is a separately supplied transition; the 2% rate governs 42→year 4 and later cash. It need not equal that first jump. If the analyst instead asserts that the stable regime already applies in year 2, the discrepancy needs an explicit explanation rather than an unnoticed switch.

  2. Average ROIC is 80/400 = 20%; b = 32/80 = 40%. New earnings are 0.125×32 = 4, while old earnings fall 6.4. Next NOPAT is 80−6.4+4 = 77.6; growth is −2.4/80 = −3%. Average ROIC×b gives 8%, using the wrong investment return and omitting erosion. Marginal ROIC×b gives 5%, which captures only new earnings. Total growth is −6.4/80 + 5% = −8%+5% = −3%.

  3. Opening capital is 72/0.18 = 400 for all three alternatives. At g = 0, b = 0, first investment 0, FCFF 72 and value 600. At g = 3%, b = 1/6, first investment 12, FCFF 60 and value 60/0.09 = 2000/3 ≈ 666.667. At g = 6%, b = 1/3, investment 24, FCFF 48 and value 800. Since 1−r/R = 1−2/3 > 0, the derivative is positive. The extra current investment reduces first cash by 12 between the two positive-growth cases but earns more than the required rate. No increase in year-1 capacity or earnings was silently inserted.

  4. K0 = 300; N1 = 0.15×300 = 45; I = 0.4×45 = 18. Depreciation is 12, capex 12+0.8×18 = 26.4, and ΔNWC = 3.6. Closing PPE is 240+26.4−12 = 254.4, NWC 63.6 and K 318. FCFF is 45−18 = 27, also 45+12−26.4−3.6. Next NOPAT is 0.12×318 = 38.16, a 15.2% decline. Old-capital earnings change by (0.12−0.15)×300 = −9; new capital contributes 0.12×18 = 2.16. Net −6.84 divided by 45 gives −15.2%; positive investment does not offset the stipulated loss of productivity.

  5. From K4 = 606.8348, N5 = 60.68348, I5 = 18.205044 and F5 = 42.478436. K5 = 625.039844; N6 = 62.5039844, I6 = 18.75119532 and F6 = 43.75278908. K6 = 643.79103932. Stable R = r makes TV6 = K6. At date 4, 42.478436/1.1 + (43.75278908+643.79103932)/1.1² = 606.8348, exactly the former TV4. Today's value remains 70340/121. Terminal share becomes approximately 62.513213%, down from 71.298886%; the underlying cash and uncertainty have not changed merely because two years acquired visible rows.

  6. K3 = 589.16 and N4 = 58.916. The three growth choices imply b = 0%, 30%, 60%; I4 = 0, 17.6748, 35.3496; F4 = 58.916, 41.2412, 23.5664; and K4 = TV4 = 589.16, 606.8348, 624.5096. Each cash-plus-continuation total is 648.076. Algebraically, N4−I4 + K3+I4 = N4+K3. With all earlier cash fixed, V0 is unchanged. Freezing I4 also fixes productive K4 and therefore N5; the claimed new growth cannot then arise under the unchanged return law. It requires a different explicitly funded or productivity-changing scenario.

  7. The positive cash's discounted growth ratio is 1.08/1.07 > 1. Terms do not decay, so the infinite sum diverges; −1000 is not its value. For the second case, b = 0.03/0.02 = 150%. That exceeds positive NOPAT and violates the stated internally financed scope. It is not a universal prohibition on investment above earnings: specify external funding, sustainability and incremental returns, revise the growth/return assumptions, or consider reducing investment. A business with only three remaining contract years can be valued using those dated cash flows and net disposal/working-capital recovery less closure obligations, with no assumed renewal. Evidence of a renewal option would support a different scenario, not an automatic perpetuity.

  8. Required b = 0.04/0.20 = 20%, so investment is 10 and first continuing FCFF 40. Operating value is 40/(0.08−0.04) = 1000; equity is 1000+12+3−100 = 915; per-share value is CU 91.5. Management obtains operating value 1250, equity 1165 and CU 116.5 per share. Its 250 operating-value overstatement is the PV of omitted reinvestment under these assumptions; borrowing for that investment would not make it free.

    A complete evidence answer addresses at least four distinct areas: (1) recurring operating earnings and a reliable tax/capital measurement base; (2) capacity, maintenance and working-capital cash that support the 20% incremental return; (3) competitive and market-size evidence supporting the duration of returns and 4% continuing growth; (4) matched currency, inflation, cash dates, risk/financing convention and claim values. Examples include customer/contracts and margin cohorts, asset/replacement budgets, receivable and inventory policies, entry or renewal evidence, and a clearly dated debt/excess-cash reconciliation. Award equivalent precise evidence designs; a list of source names without identifying the assertion to test is incomplete. The corrected arithmetic is conditional, not authenticated market value.

Teach-back

Explain to an investment committee why “71% of value is terminal, so 71% depends on eternal excess returns” is wrong for Mariner Calibration Services. Include a dated cash timeline, the final reinvestment decision, the economic-profit reconciliation and one fact that would change your confidence in the valuation.

Illustrative teaching answer

Date-4 continuation covers year 5 onward; it excludes year-4 FCFF. Year-4 investment 17.6748 creates the capital that earns NOPAT 60.68348 in year 5. With continuing return and required return both 10%, that continuation equals K4, not a perpetual excess-profit premium. Value is opening capital 500 plus the discounted finite economic profits 50, 33 and 11.44. Moving two unchanged continuation years into the explicit forecast reduces terminal share while leaving value unchanged. The continued earning capacity and replacement/NWC requirements still need evidence: a credible loss of customers or larger maintenance requirement could lower FCFF and value even without changing the heading “terminal.” A complete explanation distinguishes horizon bookkeeping from business uncertainty.

Delayed check

After 7–14 days, answer without the worked examples. (1) FCFF at date 4 is 24 and then grows 3% forever; r = 9%. Find the continuation value at date 3 and its present value at date 0. (2) Current NOPAT is 80, net investment 20, next return on that new investment 15%, and old earnings fall by 4. Find next earnings and growth. (3) A stable business has first continuing NOPAT 40 and R = r = 10%. Compare g = 0% with g = 4%, including reinvestment and value. (4) State why a finite three-year contract does not acquire an infinite life merely because a spreadsheet has a terminal-value cell.

Delayed-check answers

(1) TV3 = 24/(0.09−0.03) = 400; PV is 400/1.09³ = 400000000/1295029 ≈ 308.873392. (2) New earnings are 3; total next earnings 80−4+3 = 79, growth −1.25%. (3) At zero growth, investment is 0 and FCFF 40, giving value 400. At 4%, b = 40%, investment 16 and FCFF 24, giving 24/0.06 = 400. First NOPAT is held fixed. (4) Value the actual remaining contract cash and net closure or disposal; a renewal or new business requires evidence and its own costs, probabilities and timing.

Sources, limits and next step

The primary sources are Damodaran on operating growth and average versus marginal returns, his reinvestment/excess-return terminal-value explanation, his discussion of continuation, liquidation and competitive transition, and his stable-growth scope discussion. They are used for the identified methods, not their historical company examples, market numbers, universal risk heuristics or a claim that every firm reaches the same terminal state. All chapter cases, exercises, capital paths and lab inputs are original.

Our one-year implementation, positive-profit and deterministic capital model makes the accounting and timing visible. Actual capital vintages, uncertain adoption, financing constraints, failure, taxes and irreversible investment can change the result. The next chapter addresses risk and the required return; later chapters add capital structure, comparable prices and contingent investment choices. A defensible valuation combines those methods with evidence about a particular business.

Sources and further study

  • Aswath Damodaran, NYU Stern — The Fundamental Determinants of Growth — Operating reinvestment and growth, marginal versus average returns, and changes in earnings on existing capital; original dated capital model derives the conditions explicitly.
  • Aswath Damodaran, NYU Stern — Valuation Question 11: growth, reinvestment and excess returns — Stable reinvestment g/ROIC and the economic tradeoff between growth and available cash; growth neutrality when return equals required return.
  • Aswath Damodaran, NYU Stern — Closure in Valuation: Estimating Terminal Value, author-hosted chapter — Dated continuation versus liquidation and market multiples, competitive-advantage duration, terminal reinvestment and return assumptions, and capital plus economic-profit interpretation.
  • Aswath Damodaran, NYU Stern — The Stable Growth Rate — Relevant-market scope, real/nominal and currency consistency, and possible run-off interpretation of negative growth.
